description:
We operate as a low-friction, pragmatic team focused on first-principles problem solving. We have experience in data analysis, AI, and physical sciences.

We combine an engineering and signal processing mindset to build the models and a grounded scientific and physical logic to ensure our approach actually makes sense in the real world.

We need the right people to help us cover the other basis
If you want to build something functional and make some great connections along the way, reach out!
summary: The Hotspots is a web app that joins NASA's MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer, 2000 to 2026) and VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite, 2012 to 2026) active fire records into one burning activity calendar for any place on Earth. Raw hotspot counts jump in 2012 because VIIRS has a finer pixel, so we count active cell-days instead: days on which a satellite saw at least one qualifying fire inside a 36 km² hexagon. Before 2012, MODIS values are scaled to VIIRS units with a ratio fitted on the years both sensors flew. Every value carries a confidence level, so small places before 2012 are marked as unreliable. The app also shows a 2027 outlook from a statistical model and a demo of action advice for Italy.
details:
• Limits of the hosted demo. The app has no server: it reads precomputed files. The full world build is 2.78 GB in about 47,800 files, and free static hosting (GitHub Pages) allows 1 GB per site. So the hosted demo carries a 0.4 GB cut: the whole world at coarse resolution (hexagons of about 1,800 and 12,400 km²), the world totals and the 2027 forecast everywhere, and full detail only for Italy (36 km² hexagons, place history, calendar, Next 12 months, the Why and What to do demo, and day by day for Piedmont). Outside Italy, zooming in shows "Detail is not available here in this build" and a place shows no history. This is a hosting limit, not a limit of the method: the same app runs on the full world build locally (see Contributor.md and README.md · the-hotspots/web), and the demo video is recorded from that full build.
  • Source code: https://github.com/AlonResearch/the-hotspots
  • Project summary: README.md; Harmonization method write-up: Whitepaper.md; forecast method: Prediction.md

What it does

  • Shows a world map of H3 hexagons coloured by fire activity density. Users search a place or coordinates, or draw an area.
  • For the chosen place it shows a time strip and a calendar from 2000 to 2026, with typical and unusual months, and which hexagons make up a peak.
  • Gives every value a confidence level (high, medium, low), drawn on the strip, calendar and map.
  • Scientific mode shows the raw MODIS and VIIRS series, the uncertainty band, the check at each sensor change, the method tables and a CSV download.
  • Shows a 2027 outlook per month, clearly greyed as a forecast.
  • Works by touch on phones (tested with touch emulation in Chromium and WebKit). Daily views exist for Piedmont only.
  • The hosted app shows the whole world at coarse resolution and full detail for Italy (place history, calendar, forecast). The full world build, with detail everywhere, runs locally.

How it works

  1. Data. 660 million detections from the NASA FIRMS archive (November 2000 to 14 November 2026). We keep vegetation fires (type 0) with nominal or high confidence, on UTC days.
  2. One unit. An active cell-day is one (hexagon, day) pair with at least one qualifying detection, on the H3 grid at resolution 6 (about 36 km²). Counting days instead of detections removes most of the pixel-size difference. A larger area is the exact sum of its hexagons.
  3. Harmonization. From February 2012 the value is observed VIIRS (mean of S-NPP and NOAA-20). Before that, MODIS cell-days are multiplied by a ratio fitted on 2012 to 2019, per large region and season. Global ratios run from 2.47 to 3.06. Estimated months carry a band from resampling the fit years.
  4. Unusual months. A month is compared with the same calendar month in 2012 to 2025 (observed years only), using the 25th, 75th and 90th percentiles.
  5. Check. We predicted each overlap year from the others and compared it with what VIIRS saw. Totals came out 0.4% high (bias 1.004), and 87% of regions were within 10%.
  6. Outlook. A LightGBM quantile model on fire history gives a median and a 10% to 90% range for 67,422 areas of about 1,800 km² for each month of 2027.
  7. Italy demo. For Turin, Milan, Monte Barone and Foggia, the panel shows "Next 12 months", "Why" and "What to do".

Benefits

  • One comparable record across 26 years and a change of sensors, anchored on VIIRS so it can continue after MODIS ends.
  • Any area is an exact sum of its parts, so users can see where a peak came from.
  • Every number says how far it can be trusted, which fire managers and scientists need before acting on it.

Limits

  • Small places before 2012. MODIS saw nothing in 53% of active single-hexagon months, 47% for 7 hexagons, 41% for 49 hexagons and 15% for large regions. No ratio can recover fires MODIS never detected, and VIIRS did not exist to check a correction. So estimated months for areas under 49 hexagons, and every month before October 2002, are low confidence: faded, with no "more than usual" label.
  • Active cell-days measure how widespread and persistent burning is. They are not burned area.
  • The 2027 outlook is a model output from fire history, not a weather forecast. On two held-out years it matches the "usual value" baseline (mean absolute error 3.39 against 3.39 in 2025, 3.60 against 3.74 in 2026 January to October). Almost all its skill is the usual season of each area. The forecast code is in src/ of the repository (Prediction.md).
  • The Italy "Why" and "What to do" content is a demo. Regional driver values are profiles written by us, and the action rules are candidate rules from the literature, not validated. No soil moisture, weather or vegetation datasets are loaded.
  • The last months are provisional (near-real-time files), and November 2026 is partial.

Tools and languages

Python 3 and DuckDB with the H3 extension (data build, Parquet); TypeScript, React and Vite (app); MapLibre GL JS, deck.gl and h3-js (map); terra-draw (area drawing); LightGBM (outlook); Vitest, Playwright and axe-core (tests). The app is static JSON files with no backend. Basemap: OpenFreeMap with a bundled Natural Earth fallback.
